articles.title: China services PMI slows to 50.8 in October as price cuts meet rising costs
articles.desc: The data adds to the picture of a Chinese economy still growing but struggling with weak pricing power, which helps explain why authorities are leaning on targeted support such as this week’s expanded buyback lending. Falling selling prices alongside rising costs point to margin pressure for listed
articles.content: The data adds to the picture of a Chinese economy still growing but struggling with weak pricing power, which helps explain why authorities are leaning on targeted support such as this week’s expanded buyback lending. Falling selling prices alongside rising costs point to margin pressure for listed service companies, which may limit any equity bounce from the support measures. Firms specifically cited oil among rising input costs, a sign that higher energy prices linked to the Middle East conflict are filtering into China’s economy even as companies cannot pass them on. For the Australian dollar and commodities, the slightly firmer manufacturing output is a modest offset, but the softer services reading gives little reason to expect a stronger demand impulse from China. --- Chinese service firms are still finding customers and hiring staff, but they are cutting prices to do it while their own costs climb, a squeeze that shows up in profits before it shows up in growth. Summary: The RatingDog China General Services PMI fell to 50.8 in October from 51.6, the slowest growth in three months New business rose at a solid pace, and new export orders grew for a sixth month Employment rose for a sixth month at a faster pace, and backlogs fell for the first time in a year, helped by AI efficiencies Selling prices fell for a second month, while input costs rose at the fastest pace in five months on labour, raw material and oil costs Business confidence slipped to a three-month low The composite PMI fell to 52.0 from 52.4, despite faster manufacturing output growth China’s services sector kept growing in October but at a slower pace, a private survey showed on Wednesday. Firms cut prices to win business even though their own costs rose at the fastest rate in five months. The RatingDog China General Services PMI, compiled by S&P Global, fell to 50.8 in October from 51.6 in September. The reading stayed above the 50 mark that separates expansion from contraction, but it showed the slowest growth in activity in three months. Firms pointed to operational constraints as a factor behind the slowdown. Demand held up better than the headline suggests. New business continued to rise at a solid pace, little changed from September, extending a run of growth that began in January 2023. Firms credited wider customer bases and successful promotional efforts. New export orders rose for a sixth straight month, the longest stretch since 2024, though growth eased and was marginal. Hiring picked up. Employment rose for a sixth month, and at a faster pace than in September, as firms took on both full- and part-time staff. The extra workers, along with what firms described as efficiency gains from AI, helped reduce backlogs of work for the first time in a year. Pricing remains the main concern. Average selling prices fell for a second month as firms discounted to cope with fierce competition, although the pace of discounting eased from September. At the same time, input cost inflation hit a five-month high, driven by higher labour, raw material and oil costs, with some firms also citing social security payments. That combination points to pressure on profit margins. Business confidence stayed positive but slipped to a three-month low, as firms worried about rising costs and competition. A separate composite index, which combines manufacturing and services, fell to 52.0 from 52.4, the slowest rise in private sector output in three months. Faster growth in manufacturing output was not enough to offset the softer services expansion. RatingDog founder Yao Yu said that steady new business and stronger hiring underpinned growth at the start of the fourth quarter, but that renewed discounting and rising costs were weighing on profitability. This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

articles.title: Dubai court upholds student's dismissal over AI-written thesis
articles.desc: Student loses legal battle in Dubai after court confirms dismissal for using AI in thesis, citing academic misconduct and fabricated references.
articles.content: Dubai court upholds student's dismissal over AI-generated thesis misconduct Dubai court upholds student's dismissal over AI-written thesis Expert finds fabricated legal rulings and false references in master’s thesis Dubai: A master's student has lost the legal battle to overturn his dismissal from university over academic misconduct in his thesis, after Dubai's Court of Cassation rejected his appeal and Dh100,000 compensation claim. The court upheld the university's decision to dismiss the student and ordered him to pay legal costs and Dh2,000 in lawyers' fees. It also ruled that he would lose his appeal security deposit. The Court of Cassation issued its ruling on October 29. The student had enrolled in a master’s programme in international dispute resolution law, completed his coursework and examinations, and reached the thesis stage before the university initiated disciplinary proceedings. On December 7, 2023, the university's academic integrity officer emailed the student, alleging that his thesis was not his own work. Get updated faster and for FREE: Download the Gulf News app now - simply An investigation report dated February 8, 2024, submitted by an investigator from Birmingham Law School to the Faculty Conduct Committee, concluded that the student had used artificial intelligence to generate parts of his thesis and had copied and pasted material without properly acknowledging the sources. The committee subsequently dismissed him from the programme. His internal appeal against the decision was also rejected. The student then filed a lawsuit seeking to overturn the university's decision and its academic consequences. He asked to be reinstated, allowed to complete and submit his thesis, and awarded his master's degree. He also sought Dh100,000 in compensation for material and moral damages. The Court of First Instance dismissed his case on February 10, 2025. The Court of Appeal later appointed an expert and upheld the dismissal on July 30, 2026. In his final appeal, the student argued that AI-detection software was unreliable and could not provide conclusive evidence of misconduct. He also challenged the expert's findings, arguing that the expert had gone beyond the scope of the assignment by examining the thesis content and its legal references. He further argued that the university's decision was excessive and that a lesser disciplinary measure should have been imposed. However, the Court of Cassation found that concerns over the reliability of AI-detection tools did not invalidate the other evidence of academic misconduct. The expert had identified problems beyond the alleged use of AI, including fabricated or inaccurate legal references and judicial rulings that did not exist or had been incorrectly presented. The court considered these findings sufficient to support the conclusion that academic misconduct had occurred. It also rejected the argument that the expert had exceeded the scope of the assignment, ruling that examining the thesis content and verifying its legal references were relevant to assessing the work's integrity. The court further explained that a claim for compensation requires proof of wrongdoing, actual damage and a direct causal link between them. As the university's disciplinary decision was lawful, the student had not established the wrongdoing required to justify compensation. The Court of Cassation therefore rejected the appeal and upheld the previous judgments. AI use in academic research is not misconduct, UAE expert explains Using artificial intelligence in academic research is not academic misconduct, but submitting unverified AI-generated information, including fabricated references and fictitious court judgments, can undermine academic integrity, a UAE legal expert has warned. Dr Ammar Ali, a legal consultant specialising in AI governance , said the key issue was not whether researchers used AI, but whether they took responsibility for checking the accuracy of its output. articles.title: Sprinkler system helps contain apartment fire in downtown Seattle
articles.content: Sprinkler system helps contain apartment fire in downtown Seattle – KIRO 7 News Seattle Sprinkler system helps contain apartment fire in downtown Seattle SEATTLE — No injuries were reported after a fire broke out at an apartment complex in downtown Seattle early Tuesday morning. (SFD) crews were dispatched around 2:45 a.m. to the complex along 2nd Avenue South, near Pioneer Square. When firefighters arrived, they could see smoke coming from one of the units. Crews found the fire inside a seventh-floor apartment unit. SFD said residents did an excellent job of evacuating the building safely and quickly. The building’s sprinkler system was also effective at getting the fire under control and keeping it contained to the unit where it started. A significant amount of water was left in the fire-damaged unit and two units below it because of the sprinkler system. SFD said residents of the fire unit and the apartment directly below it will likely be displaced. So far, the department has not heard of any requests for assistance from the Red Cross. The cause of the fire remains under investigation.

articles.title: Miami a good bet for No. 1 in the initial College Football Playoff rankings, but then what?
articles.content: Miami gets top spot in first CFP rankings, followed by Georgia, Utah, Indiana - WSB-TV Channel 2 - Atlanta Miami gets top spot in first CFP rankings, but Tide at 5 and Irish at 11 bring a collective 'Huh?' It’s been a confusing college football season so far. Nobody felt that more deeply than the College Football Playoff selection committee, which raised eyebrows aplenty in its first attempt of the season to make sense of it all. Undefeated Miami received top billing in the committee's opening crack at the CFP rankings Tuesday, followed by Georgia (7-1) and undefeated Utah. From there, the 13 people in that room could have been picking from a hat. Defending champion Indiana (8-1) was ranked fourth — eight spots ahead of Ohio State (6-2), which beat the Hoosiers 19-15 last month but has since lost quarterback Julian Sayin (to say nothing of another game). At No. 5 was Alabama (6-2) — eight spots ahead of Tennessee (6-2), even though the Tide is only a few weeks removed from a 16-point loss to the Vols. At No. 6 was Kentucky (7-1), followed by Texas (6-2). UCLA, the nation's only other undefeated team, was ranked eighth. Oh, and Notre Dame. The Irish (7-1) were ranked 11th — seven spots lower than their spot in the AP Top 25 — and that ranking brought with it a simple message: As the last team that would make the bracket if the playoffs started today, they need to beat Miami on Saturday or risk slipping due to a schedule that clearly did not impress the committee. “A very, very good football team,” committee chair Hunter Yurachek said of Notre Dame. “But when you look at Notre Dame's schedule and the wins they have versus the teams ahead of them, they don't have that signature win right now.” In fact, Notre Dame's biggest game so far resulted in its only loss — 28-24 at BYU on Oct. 17. Ohio State was ranked 12th, but would be on the outside looking in because Boise State, ranked 25th, would get the Group of Six automatic bid. It would have been easy — maybe too easy — to blame the Buckeyes tumble on the fact that their offense is now in the hands of a freshman quarterback, Luke Fahey. But Yurachek said the committee was more concerned with Ohio State's defense in its 30-18 loss to a 20th-ranked USC team that hasn't impressed anyone so far. Regarding the gap between the Hoosiers and Buckeyes — and the Crimson Tide and Volunteers — Yurachek brought up a blast from last year that confused most everyone and played heavily into Miami making the final field and Notre Dame not: Head-to-head matchups don't come into play unless the teams are in the same four-team “pod,” i.e., 1-4, 5-8, 9-12. “Yes, they had that loss to Tennessee,” Yurachek said of the Tide. “But Tennessee doesn't have that same level of quality wins. Yes, they beat Alabama, but you have to go deeper” to find Tennessee's next-best win. Maybe it will come Saturday against Kentucky. Meanwhile, Yurachek said, the Tide got lots of love in the selection room for a win against Mississippi State in September before the Bulldogs disintegrated with the injury to QB Kamario Taylor. Mississippi State is currently 2-4. This is the first of six rankings that will be revealed -- one every Tuesday until the brackets are set on Sunday, Dec. 6. The playoffs start with four games on the campus of seeds 5-8 on Dec. 18-19. The final is Jan. 25 in Las Vegas. Big games Saturday will reshuffle the deck In addition to Miami-Notre Dame, key games this week include BYU at Utah for a leg up in the Big 12 race. Alabama visits No. 14 LSU in a game that will hand one contender its third loss. Also, the Kentucky-Tennessee game will either hand the Wildcats their second loss or the Vols their third. Among the biggest questions was how the selection committee would treat the SEC, which features six teams with two losses, two with one loss and no undefeateds, but also accounts for 13 of the nation's current 20 toughest schedules. articles.content: Le Havre fans demand exit of American owners amid Ligue 1 relegation fears - WSB-TV Channel 2 - Atlanta Le Havre fans call for American owners to leave after coach's suspension and president's exit With their club in turmoil, Le Havre fan groups are calling for the American owners to leave. Le Havre, founded in 1872 and considered the oldest club in French professional soccer, has plunged into a deep and unprecedented sporting crisis. Languishing at the bottom of Ligue 1, and with relegation looming, the club started the week without a coach and a president. heavy 5-1 loss against leader Paris Saint-Germain over the weekend, Le Havre announced head coach Didier Digard had been suspended, and that the board members of owner Blue Crow Sports Group had accepted the resignation of president Jean-Michel Roussier. Roussier’s resignation will be formally presented and ratified on Thursday, Le Havre said. He's led the Normandy club since 2022 while Digard was appointed in the summer of 2024. The exodus does not end there because French media have reported that sports director Demba Ba and goalkeeping coach Nicolas Douchez are also on their way out. Blue Crow acquired Le Havre in July 2025, adding it to a portfolio of soccer clubs. “In the space of just a few days, every individual who embodied this club, who helped bring it back to Ligue 1 (in 2023) and keep it there, has disappeared from its organizational structure,” three supporters groups said in a joint statement. Le Havre has two points from nine matches and the fans blame the multi-club group based in Houston for the worrying situation. “Blue Crow represents nothing in Le Havre,” they said. “Blue Crow Sports Group has dismantled (Le Havre) and demonstrates more clearly with each passing day its complete lack of understanding of how to run a football club, its history and its identity. The catastrophe that now looms is entirely their responsibility.” Le Havre’s next game is against Lorient on Sunday. “With this crucial match against Lorient approaching, the united front established between the players, the manager and the Kop (of supporters) following the match against PSG has been shattered,” the fan groups said. A former Le Havre player, Digard managed to keep the team in the topflight over the past two seasons. He leaves the club with a record of 17 wins, 20 draws and 40 losses, according to Ligue 1 statistics. The club has appointed Jaïr Karam, the academy director, as interim coach and said Yacine Alaoui would oversee administrative and sporting activities until a new chairman and CEO are appointed. articles.title: What does "Wi-Fi" stand for?
articles.desc: What do the letters in "Wi-Fi" stand for? Don't Google it. Read Entire Article
articles.content: The correct answer, the explanation, and an intriguing story await. What was the first widely used web browser? Wi-Fi: the name that never stood for anything Millions of people and even plenty of tech textbooks will tell you that Wi-Fi is short for "Wireless Fidelity." It isn't. Wi-Fi is not an acronym, and the name doesn't mean anything at all. The story starts in the late 1990s. The IEEE published the 802.11 wireless networking standard in 1997, and the faster 802.11b revision was finalized in 1999, which topped out at 11 Mbps on the 2.4 GHz band. The tech worked, but nobody was going to ask for "IEEE 802.11b" compatibility at a store. That's when the Wireless Ethernet Compatibility Alliance (WECA) started to look for something consumers could remember, so in 1999 they hired branding agency Interbrand. Interbrand is known for coming up with commercial names like Prozac, Nintendo "Wii," and Compaq. It pitched a shortlist of 10 candidates, and the alliance picked "Wi-Fi," a deliberate play on "Hi-Fi," the decades-old shorthand for high-fidelity audio. The name carried the right associations of quality and ease, without describing anything technical. Interbrand also designed the yin-yang style Wi-Fi logo. But what about the "Wireless Fidelity" confusion? Early on, some alliance board members worried that a name with no meaning would confuse people, so they attached a tagline: "The Standard for Wireless Fidelity." According to Phil Belanger, a founding member of the alliance, the tagline appeared on everything for roughly a year. He later called it a mistake that diluted the brand, and said that the phrase doesn't hold up if you take it apart. His summary of the name was blunt: "Wi-Fi doesn't stand for anything."
